entries.title: Ukraine says Musk's SpaceX limits Kyiv's Starlink access
entries.summary: Ukraine accused SpaceX of restricting use of its Starlink system, impacting Kyiv's ability to control its drones as Russian attacks continue unabated.
entries.content:
Europe

Ukraine says Musk's SpaceX limits Kyiv's Starlink access

October 14, 2026

Ukraine accused SpaceX of restricting use of its Starlink system, impacting Kyiv's ability to control its drones as Russian attacks continue unabated.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office confirmed on Wednesday that the country's military has been cut off from full access to SpaceX's Starlink satellite system as it seeks to defend itself against a now nearly five-year Russian invasion.

"Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion," said Presidential Adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov.

"Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions," he added. "Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," he added.

Starlink cut-off coincides with Trump's phantom 'energy ceasefire'

That political situation refers to US President Donald Trump's recent decision to extend Russian President Vladimir Putin a lifeline by lifting sanctions, buying Russian oil and berating Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — saying he needs to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure and that he should be replaced because "he won't make a deal" with Russia.

Trump, who considers himself a friend Putin's, has sought to blame Zelenskyy and Ukraine for skyrocketing oil and gas prices brought on by his own war in Iran and has repeatedly lashed out at the Ukrainian president, demanding he halt attacks on Russian energy facilities even as Russia continues to target Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure to terrorize the country's citizens as winter approaches.

Trump has insisted — with zero evidence — that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire" though Moscow and Kyiv both deny this.

On Tuesday evening, for instance, Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv power plant. Ukrainian officials said the Starlink outages had coincided with overnight Russian attacks.

SpaceX decision already having negative impact on Ukraine's ability to defend itself

Ukrainian troops use Starlink to conduct drone operations and internet terminals supplied by Elon Musk's company are key to operating long-distance strikes.

Presidential Advisor Beskrestnov said SpaceX had cut off access to its military-grade version of Starlink above 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), adding that Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, had been forced to cancel some missions.

"According to our ‌observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of ‌just 110–120 ​km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," a Reaction Corps representative told Reuters news agency.

A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said such limitations significantly complicate logistics and ​drone operations.

Ukraine has used Starlink terminals as an alternative to radio control for its drones as well as for ground communications since shortly after Russia launched its invasion.

Starlink's resistance to electronic jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones as well as large hexacopters that drop supplies for Ukraine's frontline troops.

Elon Musk, the world's richest man and a massive Donald Trump supporter, has, however, repeatedly shifted his stance on Ukraine since the early days of Russia's invasion.

In August, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Kyiv was looking to create an alternative to Musk's Starlink, in concert "with a European country."

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Trump's US Super Intelligence Force and AI czar Jay Clayton
entries.summary: Trump announced a new Super Intelligence taskforce with the White House AI czar Jay Clayton in charge of a group responsible for making sure the US leads international competition in artificial intelligence development.
entries.content:
October 14, 2026

Trump announced a new Super Intelligence taskforce with the White House AI czar Jay Clayton in charge of a group responsible for making sure the US leads international competition in artificial intelligence development.

"Bigger than the Industrial Revolution and the internet" — US President Donald Trump used a comparison borrowed from "many others" to describe artificial intelligence (AI) in his announcement of a "Super Intelligence Force." 

The president's move to address the rapid development of the AI industry came after he met with top AI executives at the end of September — and a month before midterm elections in November. Trump has faced intensifying pressure and warnings from business and political leaders about the mostly unregulated technology.

The name echoes Trump's September executive order renaming "Artificial Intelligence" as "Super intelligence" (SI). Jay Clayton, the director of national security and the president's new AI czar, is the task force leader. 

The task force will coordinate the government's effort "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," Trump said, and "will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."

Trump has made it clear he does not want regulation to "stifle" progress in the SI industry, and a reported charter for the group says it will work to prevent "overregulation and regulatory capture."

What the Super Intelligence Force will do

The White House has not released any information about the Super Intelligence Force, but a copy of a charter detailing the group's responsibilities was reported in The Wall Street Journal and Politico. 

The reported document shows the task force's scope is broad, but it names biosecurity and threats to the water supply as areas of focus. Recent cyberattacks have targeted critical infrastructure in the US.

The group is to work with some of the most important US government agencies, including the Pentagon, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), to develop recommendations for new laws to improve government responses.

A legal requirement for AI labs to notify the government of "breaches, hacks and jailbreaks" is to be considered, as well as the potential for automatic alerts.

"Though the labs are ultimately responsible for the risks and opportunities that their models amplify and accelerate, it is the role of the federal government to recognize and understand this era of change and to enforce our nation’s laws so that the fundamental principles of our Republic are safeguarded and advanced," the reported document says.

The charter's remit includes financial services, energy infrastructure, transportation, agriculture and emergency services. Trump said the task force would coordinate the government's engagement with consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, as well as critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, though some critics noted the omission of workers.

The task force has 120 days to deliver a report on the risks of AI, focusing on potential threats to civil liberties, cybersecurity, standards for advanced models and the impacts of possible overregulation.

Who is on the Super Intelligence Force?

Clayton, whom Trump named AI czar in early October, is to chair the task force. He told The Wall Street Journal he expected AI mechanisms to be "developed in dialogue," citing risk models the Securities and Exchange Commission, which he headed during Trump's first presidential term, and the Federal Reserve developed for the financial industry.

The reported charter also named three task force vice chairs:

  • Andrew Ferguson, chairman of the FTC
  • Emil Michael, undersecretary of defense for research and engineering
  • Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management

Ferguson is expected to oversee consumer interests and advocacy groups, according to the reported charter. His inclusion comes as the FTC investigates OpenAI, Anthropic and METR over rogue AI agents with potentially nefarious agendas.

Michael, a former tech consultant who sat on Perplexity AI's advisory board, is to oversee coordination with AI companies. Kupor is responsible for coordination with critical infrastructure providers and other industry stakeholders.

Key members of Trump's Cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, are also on the task force. The reported charter also listed David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar, and Condoleezza Rice, former secretary of state under President George W. Bush, as external members. 

The task force is to report findings and recommendations to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

Response to the task force

According to Politico, several key Republicans were not briefed on plans for the Super Intelligence Force before Trump's announcement. The task force comes as leading Republican Senators prepare major AI legislation intended to mitigate the risks AI poses.  

Democrats have criticized the president, with Lori Trahan, a member of the House of Representatives, telling CNN that Trump was "just talking about an AI force without any sort of durable strategy on how to do that through congressional authorization," which felt more like a delay tactic. 

"We should be passing legislation and guardrails around the frontier labs. And this doesn't do any of that," Trahan said.

Josh Gottheimer, another Democratic representative, told Politico he was also skeptical of Trump's motives.

"If this is the president waking up, realizing that AI risks aren’t a hoax, and is taking concrete action to protect America, then great," Gottheimer said. "If this is just a PR diversion and an attempt to protect his family’s investments, then I have a massive problem."

Edited by: Davis VanOpdorp

entries.title: Trump announces plans for major oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland
entries.summary: The US president has claimed Greenland holds vast and easily accessible oil reserves without providing evidence or details. His announcement follows a deal expanding the US military presence on the Arctic island.
entries.content:
Denmark

Greenland: Trump touts major oil, gas, mineral exploration

October 14, 2026

The US president has claimed Greenland holds vast and easily accessible oil reserves without providing evidence or details. His announcement follows a deal expanding the US military presence on the Arctic island.

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said major oil, gas and mineral exploration was set to begin in Greenland.

His announcement follows a security agreement between the United States, Denmark and the Arctic island's leaders.

What has Trump said about Greenland's resources?

Trump offered no details about which companies would be involved, where exploration would take place or when operations would begin.



"Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

He also claimed that experts believed Greenland held some of the world's largest deposits of easily accessible oil, without providing evidence. 

Greenland is believed to hold substantial untapped oil reserves, but their commercial viability remains uncertain due to high extraction costs, harsh Arctic conditions and environmental restrictions. No commercial oil production has been established in Greenland.

Greenland has significant mineral resources, including rare earth elements used in electronics, renewable energy technologies and military equipment.

The island has also attracted interest for its potential oil and gas reserves, although exploration in the harsh Arctic environment presents considerable technical and economic challenges.

In August, reports that a US oil company was preparing operations in a remote part of eastern Greenland prompted unease among residents and local authorities.

Trump did not say whether his announcement was connected to those activities.

Why is Greenland strategically important to the US?

In the same post, Trump described Greenland's strategic location as "second to none" for US and European security.

"Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland," he claimed, adding that US defenses there would be able to intercept missiles, drones and other weapons.

Greenland lies along one of the shortest routes between Russia and North America, making it strategically important for missile detection and defense.

Its location is also significant for Trump's proposed "Golden Dome" missile defense system.

Melting Arctic ice has meanwhile increased interest in potential new shipping routes through the region.

What does the US security deal with Greenland involve?

In September, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement aimed at easing tensions after Trump's repeated threats to take control of the island, including by force.

Under the 10-page agreement, Washington will establish two additional military bases, at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig in the east.

The US already operates the Pituffik Space Base in northern Greenland.

The agreement expands the American military presence and provides for cooperation on missile defense, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty over Greenland and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination.

Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.

Trump's earlier demands for US control of the island had strained relations between Washington and Copenhagen, both NATO allies.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

entries.title: Fact check: Misleading graph about alleged Russian bot activity
entries.summary: Did attacks on Russian data centers reduce bot activity around Germany's AfD? A viral graph claims they did. But it contains significant inconsistencies and provides no evidence to support the claim.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Fact check: Viral graph suggests drop in alleged Russian bot activity

October 14, 2026

Did attacks on Russian data centers reduce bot activity around Germany's AfD? A viral graph claims they did. But it contains significant inconsistencies and provides no evidence to support the claim.

After Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers operated by the Russian technology company Yandex, claims began circulating online that the strikes had disrupted or even halted the activity of Russian propaganda bots. These accounts are often accused of spreading disinformation or artificially amplifying content on social media.

During the Warsaw Security Forum, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also suggested that the attacks on Yandex data centers had disrupted bot activity, saying "there was less hate, less division, and fewer provocations [because] there were fewer bots."  In response to BBC Verify, Zelenskyy's office said that, rather than referring to reduced bot activity, the president was "talking about the atmosphere on social media." The office added that it had seen "reports of fewer provocative and hateful comments" from many social media users.

So far, however, there is no clear evidence linking the attacks to a decline in bot activity. According to Josef Holnburger, managing director of the Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), there is currently "no decline in Russian disinformation activities that could be explained by the attack on Yandex data centers." CeMAS systematically monitors such campaigns.

European lawmaker shares graph without evidence on X

Nevertheless, a misleading graph has been circulated as supposed evidence. It was shared, for example, by Czech Member of the European Parliament Tomáš Zdechovský. His post was viewed more than four million times on X. He suggested that the graph might demonstrate a decline in "online activity around AfD," although he did not specify what kind of activity he meant. In reality, the graph most likely demonstrates nothing at all. 

The German-language graph is titled "Daily activity over 3 months." It appears to show activity remaining relatively stable before dropping sharply in early October, roughly coinciding with the attacks on Yandex data centers. However, nothing in the graph itself indicates that this relates to AfD-related online activity.

No source and faulty scaling

The same applies to the graph's underlying data. It is unclear which data were used. No source is provided, nor is there any explanation of the data collection process or calculation method for the alleged "activity," which initially ranges between 6,000 and 7,000 before falling below 3,000.

Particularly striking is that the graph extends to October 15. Its final data point appears to correspond to October 14 – a date that was still in the future when the graph first appeared online on October 11. Data for a future date cannot exist.

The graph also contains scaling errors on both the X and Y axes. For example, on the Y axis, the distance between 2,500 and 3,000 is smaller than the other 500-unit intervals. Because the Y axis does not begin at zero, the decline is visually exaggerated. On the X axis, equal periods of time are represented by unequal distances.

It is also unclear which platforms were analyzed and how the variable "activity" was calculated. The absence of a known data source, the inaccurate scaling, and the inclusion of "future" values strongly suggest that this is not a meaningful graph based on factual data and sound statistical methods.

AI involvement cannot be proven, but is possible

It is unclear whether AI was used to create the graph. Given the errors and the apparent "hallucination" of presenting future data, AI involvement cannot be ruled out.

Misleading and error-filled graphs, some of which may have been AI-generated, appear regularly.  German public broadcaster BR's #Faktenfuchs team recently reported on one such graph that falsely depicted industrial production in Germany (article in German). False or fabricated graphs can lend credibility to unsupported claims.

The identity of the graph's creator remains unknown.

What do Cloudflare data actually show?

Cloudflare data are also frequently cited in connection with claims of declining bot activity. However, according to CeMAS managing director Holnburger, there is a misunderstanding about what Cloudflare's report actually means. Cloudflare provides services to many websites that block traffic assessed as non-human. Automated web traffic is common and includes, for example, crawlers that check websites for freshly published content. Search engines, including Yandex, rely on these crawlers. Other bots may be used for spam in comment sections.

In a message to #Faktenfuchs Holnburger writes, "a decline in bot activity on websites is something entirely different from a decline in inauthentic behavior by social bots on social networks."

Referring to Cloudflare data, he added: "When looking at overall activity from Russian IP addresses on servers using Cloudflare services, there is no major decline in bot activity." Furthermore, there is no reason to assume that the infrastructure used by disinformation-related social bots would be hosted on Yandex data centers. "It is more likely that these systems are distributed across many different providers," Holnburger writes.

The article was originally written in German and adapted into English by Alima de Graaf

This article is part of a collaboration between Germany's public broadcasting fact-checking teams ARD-Faktenfinder, BR24 #Faktenfuchs and DW Fact check.

entries.title: Do non-German nationals commit more crimes than Germans?
entries.summary: People without German passports appear more frequently in German police crime statistics than German nationals. A new study explains why.
entries.content:
Germany

Do non-German nationals commit more crimes than Germans?

October 14, 2026

People without German passports appear more frequently in German police crime statistics than German nationals. A new study explains why.

Every year, when the Federal Criminal Police Office publishes the police crime statistics, theAlternative for Germany (AfD) — a party that is, in part, right-wing extremist — pays particularly close attention. They are looking for crimes committed by refugees, migrants and foreigners living in Germany.

But studies by media scholars show that 95% of the AfD's press releases focus on non-German suspects, while crimes involving German suspects are almost completely ignored.

However, the common narrative of the AfD — that non-Germans are inherently much more violent — is simply not true.

In a new research paper, Susann Prätor, a sociologist, criminologist and professor at the Lower Saxony Police Academy, has taken a very close look at crime data in Germany, together with her colleagues from the University of Zurich and the Lower Saxony Criminological Research Institute.

She looked not only at officially reported crime — that is, all offenses that appeared in police crime statistics — but also at unreported crime: These are all offenses that are not reported or detected, and therefore do not appear in any official statistics but are identified through representative surveys.

"According to police crime statistics, people who do not have German citizenship commit crimes more frequently than German citizens. However, studies into unreported cases show that non-German nationals are twice as likely to be reported. Differences between the two groups are also evident in crimes that go unreported, but they are significantly less pronounced," Prätor told DW.

German offenders are reported to the police much less frequently

Crimes committed by foreign nationals are therefore twice as likely to appear in police crime statistics as crimes committed by Germans.

These statistics record all reported cases and do not specify whether the allegations prove to be true.

When the statistics are adjusted for the bias in the reporting of crimes, foreigners are no longer 2.6 times more likely to commit crimes than Germans, but only 1.7 times more likely. This figure is also consistent with the results of studies on unreported juvenile violent crime. According to these studies, foreign youths are about 1.6 times as likely to commit violent crimes as German youths.

Other factors affecting crime include age and gender. Young men make up a larger proportion of the foreign-born population, and young men are the group most prone to criminal behavior across all societies.

According to Prätor, "categories such as being young, male, poorly educated and having a history of violence are factors that increase the likelihood of violent behavior. A certain concept of masculinity also plays a role, wherever that may come from. But we do not see culture as a factor, contrary to the prejudice that masculinity and violence play a greater role in other cultures."

Prätor points to a survey on attitudes toward violence. According to the survey, 5% of German youths view violence positively. Among those without a German passport, the figure is 10%.

The criminologist has identified a crucial factor: "Family upbringing plays an important role in shaping attitudes toward violence, because these attitudes are formed in the home. If I experience violence in my own home, I will have a different relationship to violence than if I hadn't experienced it," said Prätor.

Germany is, however, on the right track, says Prätor, even if it doesn't always feel that way. "Fifty or sixty years ago, parental violence was much more common in child-rearing than it is today. Acts of violence committed by young people are also far less frequent than they were in the 1990s or the early 2000s."

Prätor emphasizes that it is important to bring objectivity to the debate. A good illustration of this is a look at police records of serious violent crimes — such as aggravated assault, manslaughter, or murder. "Of every 100 German citizens, 0.2% commit violent crimes; among non-German nationals, the figure is 0.6%."

However, Prätor points out that "more than 99% of the people living here in Germany — whether of German or non-German origin — the overwhelming majority in this country do not commit any serious violent crimes at all."

Germany must do more to prevent crime

Prätor also trains prospective police officers. She wants to send the message to policymakers that they should place greater emphasis on the positive aspects of migration. She argues that the debate on immigration is far too negative, largely due to an overly narrow focus on police crime statistics. The vast majority of non-Germans integrate exceptionally well, she says.

She wants the government to invest more money in prevention.

"By starting as early as possible with children and adolescents: strengthening social skills as early as preschool, building on that in school and responding when incidents of violence do occur. It's also important to invest in infrastructure and recreational activities in certain regions. After all, a key factor in youth violence — regardless of background — is that young people lack a meaningful daily structure," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football
entries.summary: Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and new faces at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for greater structure globally.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football

October 14, 2026

Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and new faces at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for greater structure globally.

At first glance, women's football is healthier than ever. A recent report by FIFPRO, football's global players' union, said worldwide revenue is expected to reach over $1bn (€894m) in 2027. The World Cup in Brazil, a first in South America, will be the last with 32 teams and is expected to be the most watched and biggest revenue-generating women's tournament ever.

The good news continues with the U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where the tournament is being held every year for five straight years. Germany, France, Spain, Brazil, the United States and defending champions North Korea are all at the 2026 edition of a competition whose reputation continues to grow.

"You can just see where the game is going, which is so exciting," US head coach Ciara Crinion told FIFA. "The level has just gone up. We have to continue to stay with that and compete as well. [The U-17 Women's World Cup] almost feels like that first stepping stone in a major tournament for young players, and now you see how serious it is taken."

Puerto Rico, Australia and Argentina are making their debuts. For Puerto Rico, qualification is a moment of history as no football team in the men's or women's game has ever reached a World Cup tournament before.

"We've embraced this idea of being Puerto Rico's first team to qualify for a World Cup," head coach Andres Mirabelli told FIFA. Alongside national development plans, player recruitment was aided by a diaspora of nearly four million in the United States, perhaps the strongest place for women's football in the world. According to FIFPRO, the regional football average salary in North America is $5,940 (€5,547) per month, which is far higher than any other continent.

Women's game falling short on global standards

But even for the handful of players who make it out of these youth tournaments to a professional career, creating a living out of the beautiful game remains a real challenge. The aforementioned FIFPRO report details that many professional female players across the world barely earn minimum wage, with some even falling below it.

The report, which sourced its data from player surveys across the world, found that only 66% of professional players are paid for 12 months a year. The global average salary is $2,600 (€2,300) a month, but the range varies drastically across the world. In Eastern Europe, for example, that average is just $880 per month. In Africa, it is just $432, but in North America it is just under $6,000.

"I think what you also find in the women's game is the gaps are not just between the top five leagues and the rest. There is a gap there, but even within leagues themselves [there is one]," FIFPRO head of research and strategy for women's football Frankie Brown told DW. "In some of the other leagues you're dealing with teams that are operating professionally, so will be paying their players on a reasonable wage, and playing in the same league as them you'll have players that are on amateur contracts and not being paid at all."

With economic and job security an issue for many, the report reveals that psychological stress factors are now the second main reason many consider leaving football.

"This is one of the most concerning parts of the report," Alex Culvin, the director of women's football at FIFPRO, said in a statement. "Of the 49% of women’s football players considering leaving the sport early, 46% cited their mental health as the reason. In interviews, players say the sport's growth brings new pressures — including extra workload and social media abuse — but that clubs do not have the necessary safeguards in place to support these changes. We want clubs and national associations to provide mandatory mental health support focused on wellbeing, which is independent of sporting performance objectives."

FIFPRO's report is asking FIFA to set a so-called floor for the women's game so that minimum standards in key areas such as contracts, pensions and health can be enforced. Perhaps inspiration can be taken from the labor deal the WNBA agreed in 2026. It was long-negotiated deal that ultimately sent a message to female athletes everywhere to push for better pay, conditions and a greater share of the revenue they help generate.

"It is positive that average salaries are increasing for some players and that more are earning a satisfactory wage, but it’s important to note that there is a huge disparity in pay across regions," said Culvin.

"There is also an imbalance in conditions, not only across the globe but also within regions; in Europe, for example, the difference in standards between the east and west is enormous. This is a gulf we need to work hard to narrow; the growth in the most advanced markets must not be completely isolated from the rest of the industry.

Germany aiming to be example of development

With high hopes for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and recent moves to increase professional football domestically, Germany is aiming to become an example for structural improvement in women's football. Hosting the Euros in 2029 certainly gives them an incentive to improve standards.

While salaries are in the upper tier - in the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year - the process of structural development in the country is still in its infancy. A new German FA (DFB) rule shows that even basic professional structures are still being established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

"The facilities and the staff members," Nicole Anyomi told DW were a factor in her making a recent move to London City Lionesses. "We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

Ultimately, the faster the game grows the greater need to close the gaps.

"Despite playing on different continents, players are connected by their precarity," Culvin said. "The redistribution systems in women's football need to be more effective, touching more players and supporting a more sustainable ecosystem."

Edited by: Matt Pearson

entries.title: The hidden treasure in discarded wearable and fast tech
entries.summary: Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.
entries.content:
ClimateGlobal issues

Unused mini fans, vapes and smartwatches: A critical mineral gold mine

October 14, 2026

Sales of fast tech like mini fans and disposable e-vapes, as well as wearable health tech such as heart monitors and smartwatches are soaring. They're creating a new e-waste problem but are full of hidden treasure.

From mini fans and the cheap chargers to smartwatches bought as part of a New Year's health kick, some 44% of Europeans own at least six "fast-tech" gadgets. And more than half say they keep unused and broken e-waste items languishing at home or throw them in the regular trash instead of recycling. 

That's according to a new report by Brussels-based e-waste association WEEE Forum. It describes fast tech, which is booming, as charging and lighting devices under €10 (circa $11), high-tech items like power banks and fitness trackers, and gadgets and lifestyle appliances like cheap mini blenders and fans, as well as single-use electronic vapes. 

"So, these electronics are a bit like fast fashion," Magdalena Charytanowicz, WEEE Forum's Communication Manager, told DW.

Nearly 40% of buyers recalled discarding a fast-tech item without using it at all or within a month of buying it, and nearly 60% said they had used a product for no longer than six months. Yet the vast majority of respondents were generally satisfied with their gadgets despite short-lived functionality.

This suggests consumers accept the "fast-tech bargain" of poor quality that "does the job for a while" and is easily replaced — similar to fast fashion — according to the report.

The Great Wall of e-waste and what to do about it

About 62 million tons of electronics are discarded worldwide annually. "That's the Great Wall of China of e-waste that is produced every year," noted Charytanowicz, adding that the figure is set to grow to 82 million by 2030.

In Europe, roughly 40% of electronic waste is recycled, yet the rate worldwide is just 17%. This means valuable materials are lost, while electronic waste ends up polluting the environment. 

In 2022, a million tons of critical raw materials were embedded in the 10.7 million tons of e-waste generated across Europe, including manganese, gold, copper and aluminum.

These materials are at "the center of geopolitical tensions," Charytanowicz said, referring to escalating global tensions over access to rare earths and other critical minerals.

"Even the smallest" devices are worth recycling if they contain a circuit board or battery, she said.

Groups like WEEE Forum say more awareness raising is needed on how to dispose of cheap electronic devices, and that recycling should be made as easy as possible.

But the best way to reduce a product's environmental impact is to extend its lifespan through better design and repair, as recycling raw materials is energy intensive. 

Charytonawicz said clearer, harmonized EU rules now under consideration could help improve e-waste collection. The bloc's 20-year-old directive is "not really adapted to the changing reality," she said.

Healthcare's increasing digital waste problem

Another growing area of e-waste is digital healthcare. While devices such as diabetes sensors and blood pressure monitors are "transforming healthcare," many are designed to be disposable.

A study published in Nature in December 2025 found sales of wearable healthcare electronics, for example, could reach 2 billion devices annually by 2050, and generate a million tons of e-waste.

Jeremy Faludi, associate professor of sustainable design engineering at TU Delft in the Netherlands, says making health tech — particularly digital devices used in, or issued by hospitals — recyclable or reusable comes with some "much bigger challenges" than normal electronics.

That's in part due to the potential for patient contamination, particularly with digital surgical devices that come into contact with blood or other bodily fluids.

"The way that a lot of things are designed now, you can't recover the stuff because it can't be easily sterilized without the electronics," said Faludi.

He worked on the Digital Health in Circular Economy (DiCE) project, an EU-funded initiative, to help redesign digital healthcare devices to "recover critical materials and reduce environmental impacts without compromising patient safety."

A modular design, for example, allows electronic components to be separated from the parts that need to be replaced between patients, making devices easier to reuse.

The four-year DiCE project, which included citizens, hospitals and manufacturers across nine EU countries, found reusable ECG cables — which connect patients to heart-monitoring equipment — cut environmental impacts by up to 81-94%, for example. The sets are usually designed for single use.

Rules around medical waste can also make reuse and recycling more difficult, particularly when requirements differ between countries and often come down to perceived rather than actual risk, Faludi added. He says some 85% of hospital trash is not infectious but everything ends up in the same bins. Better sorting as well as EU-wide regulations around treating non-infectious hospital waste would help here.

'Green nudges' help citizens to recycle

Like with other tech, consumer health devices such as blood pressure and glucose monitors often risk being forgotten in drawers or ending up in the wrong waste, simply because people do not know how to dispose of them, said Charytanowicz of WEEE Forum, which is also involved in DiCE.

Pilot schemes in Belgium, Spain and Slovenia that offered free postal returns and collection machines in public places found that more than 60% of people were willing to return unwanted devices if it was a straightforward process.

"What's really important is the convenience so that it can be integrated in your daily routines," said Charytanowicz, adding that "nudges"such as messages that recycling a device could help the health of another person motivate people to "do the right thing."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Germany news: Nord Stream sabotage suspect's trial opens
entries.summary: A Ukrainian man is going on trial in Hamburg in the case of a 2022 attack on major gas pipelines. At the same time, Chancellor Merz is expected to give a major policy statement. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Nord Stream sabotage suspect's trial opens

Published October 14, 2026last updated October 14, 2026

A Ukrainian man is going on trial in Hamburg in the case of a 2022 attack on major gas pipelines. At the same time, Chancellor Merz is expected to give a major policy statement. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Serhii K. is believed to be one of several people involved in the September 2022 explosion at the Nord Stream gas pipelines
  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz is scheduled to deliver a major policy statement amid sinking popularity and coalition infighting
  • Germany's foreign minister will meet his Bulgarian counterpart following drone attacks in the Black Sea

Here is a roundup of all the headlines across Germany on Wednesday, October 14:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click hereto add DW as a Preferred Source on Google

Skip next section Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%

Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%

Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023, as fuel and heating oil prices surged.

The Federal Statistical Office confirmed its preliminary estimate, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.

The increase was again driven by energy prices, said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting higher costs at gas stations and for heating oil.

Energy prices rose 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest annual increase since February 2023. That followed increases of 10.5% in August and 8.3% in July.

Motor fuel prices jumped 37.1%, while heating oil rose 74.9%. Firewood, wood pellets and other solid fuels became 15.6% more expensive.

However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating cost 1% less.

The office attributed those declines partly to government measures implemented since the start of the year.

Skip next section Nord Stream sabotage trial draws protesters

Nord Stream sabotage trial draws protesters

The trial of a Ukrainian man accused of leading the operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 has begun in Hamburg.

The 50-year-old, identified under German privacy rules as Serhii K., faces charges including a war crime, causing explosions, destroying structures and disrupting public services.

DW correspondent Matthew Moore was there as court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg.

A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist". One participant from Germany told DW that they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."

Inside, a Ukrainian student also told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii K.

"Serhii K is a hero." In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, K faces a lengthy prison sentence.

Prosecutors allege that he planned the attack with other Ukrainian military personnel on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state bodies. They say the aim was to prevent Russia from using gas export revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.

Serhii K., who was arrested in Italy last year, denies involvement. Ukraine's government has also denied any role in the attack.

Skip next section Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms

Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to outline Germany's priorities on Ukraine, European defense and economic competitiveness in a parliamentary address ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.

His government statement is scheduled for 14:05 local time (12:05 UTC), followed by a 90-minute debate. EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday, with the Middle East, the bloc's next long-term budget and EU enlargement also on the agenda.

After the speech, the opposition Greens are set to put forward two motions calling for faster bloc enlargement and stronger measures to counter economic coercion and protect the bloc's market.

Merz's address follows a more domestic-focused speech on planned reforms at an employers' conference in Berlin on Tuesday. There, he said he would press ahead with changes to Germany's welfare system even at the expense of his own popularity, arguing that younger generations stood to benefit.

Skip next section Anti-nuclear activists block waste convoy

Anti-nuclear activists block waste convoy

Police in the town of Dorsten, just north of the city of Essen, said that they had detained three people who were blocking the A31 motorway.

The group was attempting to stop trucks carrying radioactive waste.

After repelling down from a bridge above the highway, they unfurled a banner reading "stop this crap."

The incident was the latest in Germany's decades-long protest movement against nuclear weapons and atomic energy.

Although the last of the country's nuclear power stations went offline in 2023, transporting and storing the waste remains a divisive topic.

This particular convoy was headed for a facility in Ahaus, near the Dutch border. Authorities believe it could take until 2028 to safely store all the remaining waste from Germany's decommissioned atomic reactors.

Skip next section Suicide rate increased significantly in 2025

Suicide rate increased significantly in 2025

The suicide rate in Germany has continued to climb, according to official statistics just released by the Federal Ministry of Health.

In 2025, at least 11,334 people killed themselves in Germany. That is a 9.3% increase on the previous year, and 15.6% higher than the average over the past decade.

This is higher than the number of deaths due to traffic accidents, AIDS, murder and manslaughter put together.

The data shows that this is partly due to more women (a 17.9% increase since 2021) taking their own lives, though most suicides are still carried out by men. The increase is also due to an increase in assisted suicides for the elderly and infirm, amounting to over 1,000 people.

In a 2020 decision, Germany's top court struck down a 2015 ban on organized assisted dying providers like Switzerland's Dignitas, and called on the Bundestag to create regulations for the practice. However, lawmakers have declined thus far to do so, putting assisted suicide in a legal gray area in Germany. Direct euthanasia by a single doctor remains illegal.

In August, the Health Ministry proposed reforms such as a national suicide prevention hotline, more support for local and state networks, as well as the creation of a federal office for suicide prevention.

However, medical groups and charities have both said that the proposed €1.4 million ($1.6 million) budget would come nowhere never covering such a scheme long-term.

Editor's note: If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://www.befrienders.org/

Skip next section Proposed sugar tax faces criticism

Proposed sugar tax faces criticism

According to German media reports, the ruling coalition of Chancellor Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Social Democrats (SPD) has found a compromise for a planned tax increase on sugar.

The law would impact sugar drinks in particular, and is set to come into effect on July 1 of next year. There is reportedly going to be an exception for small-scale producers.

CDU state premier of Hesse, Boris Rhein, slammed the plan on Wednesday. Rhein told the Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper that this "expensive tax" (a phrase that rhymes in German) would simply result in companies passing on the extra expense to consumers.

Rhein accused the coalition of pretending the measure was about health when really it was so "the populace can continue to plug up holes in the federal budget at the cash register."

Skip next section Nord Stream sabotage suspect goes on trial in Hamburg

Nord Stream sabotage suspect goes on trial in Hamburg

The much anticipated trial of Serhii K., whose last name is withheld due to Germany's privacy laws, will begin in Hamburg today. 

K. is accused by investigators of leading a group comprising professional divers, an explosives expert, and a boat skipper who plotted to travel to the remote section of the Nord Stream gas pipelines off the Danish coast and blow them up.

The series of explosions ruptured Nord Stream 1, which Moscow had switched off a month earlier, and destroyed Nord Stream 2, which had yet to come into operation at the time.

A former Ukrainian military officer, K's case has led some investigators to point at Kyiv as orchestrating the entire plan, as the pipelines controversially delivered Russian natural gas to Europe.

The attack came seven months after Russia's fullscale invasion of Ukraine, when European countries were taking steps to drastically decrease their reliance on Russian fuel.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has vehemently denied any official connection to the attack.

K. was apprehended in Italy in 2025 and extradited to Germany. His specific charges are: being an accomplice to a war crime by attacking civil energy infrastructure, disruption of public services, causing an explosion and destroying structures.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

A hearty guten Morgen from the DW newsroom in Bonn.

It's a day for political and legal battles today, as a man suspected of being part of a conspiracy to blow up a major gas pipeline between Russia and Europe goes on trial.

Later, Chancellor Friedrich Merz will give a sweeping address on his future policies as government approval ratings sink to a record low.

All this and more is coming up in our Germany blog.

entries.title: Iran: Political infighting deepens as economic woes mount during war
entries.summary: Hardliners are stepping up pressure on Iran's government and calling for Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's removal. The oil minister resigned, but that's doing little to ease the pressure on President Masoud Pezeshkian.
entries.content:
Iran

Political infighting in Iran deepens as economic woes mount

October 14, 2026

Hardliners are stepping up pressure on Iran's government and calling for Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi's removal. The oil minister resigned, but that's doing little to ease the pressure on President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Hardliners are piling the pressure on Iran’s government and calling for the removal of Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad’s resignation is also failing to ease the pressure on President Masoud Pezeshkian.

As the war continues and diplomatic efforts to find a solution make little headway, the internal power struggle is intensifying. President Pezeshkian’s government is the focus of mounting tension.

Hardliners in Iran's parliament are pushing for impeachment proceedings against Araghchi. A trigger for the discontent was Araghchi's meeting with US negotiators on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. Critics accuse the foreign minister of holding the talks without official authorization.

In a letter, Tehran lawmaker Amirhossein Sabeti informed parliamentary speaker Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf that he had registered a motion to impeach Araghchi on parliament’s online portal. Lawmaker Hossein-Ali Haji-Deligani also said parliament could use its oversight powers, including impeachment proceedings.

A structural problem within Iran’s power system

"When the regime is forced to negotiate, as it is in the current situation and in talks with the United States, the supreme leader or the hardline core of power avoids taking responsibility and shifts it onto elected institutions and moderate forces within the government," political analyst Ali Afshari, who lives in the United States, told DW.

Hardliners can use this approach to attack moderate factions over decisions that were previously agreed upon within the power apparatus, Afshari said.

He added that hardliners serve an important function within the Islamic Republic.

"The role of hardliners in the Islamic Republic is to influence public opinion, the political system's traditional supporters and the values of the Islamic Republic in both domestic and foreign policy," he said.

Hardliners held a parliamentary majority during the implementation of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), the 2015 nuclear deal, and voiced their political opposition. Their resistance, however, ultimately did not affect the signing of the agreement.

"The Foreign Ministry is not a decision-maker. It implements what the government asks of it — and Araghchi is operating within that framework," Afshari said.

Lawmakers must first collect a set number of signatures to move forward with impeachment proceedings.

The lucrative business of oil

The timing of the latest move is significant: Iran's government finds itself under enormous economic pressure.  Meanwhile, oil exports, which are one of the country's key sources of revenue, have fallen sharply as a result of the US blockade.

The resignation of Oil Minister Paknejad adds to the pressure. Officially, he stepped down for personal reasons.

Umud Shokri, an energy strategist, geopolitical analyst and energy security expert, casts doubt that a change at the helm of the Oil Ministry would alter the situation. Iran relies on networks that enable it to export oil despite sanctions, Shokri said. Opaque structures have become entrenched, making it harder for the government to control key revenue streams.

Circumventing sanctions has become a lucrative business for certain factions within Iran's political system, he said.

"By law, these revenues should be under state control. But we know that has not been the case for years," Shokri said.

Economic opacity has deepened during the sanctions period, he added, under the pretext of national security and protecting the population.

Private actors with close ties to the country's centers of power, particularly the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have developed methods to sell oil to the armed forces through hidden channels. Neither the prices nor the commissions charged or the total sums involved are transparent.

"The government has only limited influence over these transactions. The Revolutionary Guards, in particular, would organize and control such deals," Shokri said.

Analysts have signaled that political and economic situation could likely deteriorate further in the coming days and weeks.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: India news: 'Cockroach' leaders sent to judicial custody amid protest crackdown
entries.summary: Three of India's Cockroach movement leaders will spend five days in jail over charges of trespassing into what was until recently a designated protest site. In other news, Marco Rubio is set to visit India. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India news: 'Cockroach' leaders sent to judicial custody

Published October 14, 2026last updated October 14, 2026

Three of India's Cockroach movement leaders will spend five days in jail over charges of trespassing into what was until recently a designated protest site. In other news, Marco Rubio is set to visit India. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • 'Cockroach' party leaders sent to five days in judicial custody
  • Boat capsizes in state of Bihar killing at least 13, mostly children
  • US Secretary of State Marco Rubio set to visit India next week

Here are the top headlines from India on Wednesday, October 14: 

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Activist groups attempt to march towards Jantar Mantar

Activist groups attempt to march towards Jantar Mantar

Activists of the Students' Federation of India (SFI) and the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) on Wednesday tried to march towards the former designated protest venue of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi. However, they were stopped by authorities at barricades.

Students of the leftist organizations raised Slogan such as "reclaim Jantar Mantar" and "Gyanesh Kumar must resign," refering to the Chief Election Commissioner of India who is facinf mass Protests over allegations of misconduct.

Calls to reclaim Jantar Mantar came two days after Delhi Police delisted the centrally-located grounds as a designated protest site.

Skip next section Air India Frankfurt-Delhi flight diverted after bomb threat

Air India Frankfurt-Delhi flight diverted after bomb threat

An Air India Aircraft flying from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to the Indian city of Jaipur on Wednesday, following a bomb threat, news agency Press Trust of India reported.

The Boeing aircraft made an emergency landing at the Jaipur International Airport and was immediately escorted to a designated isolation bay. Airport authorities alerted the police about the emergency landing and the bomb threat.

Meanwhile, Indian media reported that the airplane's pilot issued the emergency code of '7500,' the internationally recognized aviation code for hijacking or unlawful interference. The aircraft has since been cleared.

India's aviation regulator is currently probing the incident, Hindustan Times reported citing sources.

Skip next section US' Marco Rubio to visit India next week

US' Marco Rubio to visit India next week

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will visit India's western cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar next week to meet with senior government officials, in what will be his second official visit to the country this year. 

Rubio and Indian officials will discuss strengthening the US-India strategic partnership, prospects for enhanced energy cooperation, and exchange views on regional and global dynamics, the US Department of State said in a media note.

"Secretary Rubio will also meet with business leaders to promote opportunities for commercial investment and economic cooperation," it said.

Mumbai, a coastal city in the western state of Maharashtra is India's financial capital while Jamnagar is an industrial City in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat.

Ties between New Delhi and Washington have been rocky since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House, over issues including his repeated claim of brokering an India-Pakistan ceasefire and ​a US military attack on a ship off Oman that killed three Indian seafarers.

New Delhi has also raised concerns over US legislation allowing Trump to impose ⁠tariffs ​of up to 100% on countries that purchase Russian ​energy, part of Washington's efforts to pressure Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine.

Skip next section 'We will reclaim it': Rahul Gandhi on Jantar Mantar

'We will reclaim it': Rahul Gandhi on Jantar Mantar

Indian Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi criticized the arrest of Cockroach Janta Party leader Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka for allegedly trespassing into the the delisted protest site of Jantar Mantar a day ago.

"Waving the Tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice," he said in a post on X, reacting to the news of the duo being sent to judicial custody for five days.

"Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India. We will reclaim it," he said.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: Can 'cockroaches' threaten Modi's political grip?

IN DEPTH: Can 'cockroaches' threaten Modi's political grip?

India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) may have anticipated pushback from the government after its first round of protests in July, but the scale of barricading and detentions that greeted its leaders in a fortress-like New Delhi on October 10 was unlike anything they had anticipated.

Thousands detained, leaders arrested on arrival, and a capital under lockdown: The youth-led protests against the election chief have the attention of the Indian government. But experts say toppling it is another matter.

Read the full story here.

Skip next section WATCH: AI fakes targeting women at CJP protests

WATCH: AI fakes targeting women at CJP protests

AI-generated women are being inserted into real footage of CJP protests in India.

Some accounts used the fakes to promote paid explicit content, while others shared them to mock protesters and question their credibility.

Skip next section Boat capsizes in Bihar, killing 13

Boat capsizes in Bihar, killing 13

A boat capsized in the river Ganges in the eastern state of Bihar, drowning at least 13 people, authorities said on Wednesday.

News agency Press Trust of India reported that all of the deceased were children under the age of 15. At least six others on board were rescued.

The boat overturned on Tuesday night while carrying passengers to a feast in a neighboring village across the river, authorities told local media.

Rescue operators have retrieved the vessel and are conducting an investigation.

Several regional and national leaders expressed their grief over the incident. Prime Minister Narendra Modi said it was "deeply painful," offering his condolences to the bereaved families.

"I pray for the speedy recovery of all those injured. The local administration is assisting those affected," Modi said through his office's account on X.

Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary said the News was "heartbreaking and soul-wrenching."

"Instructions have been given to the administration to swiftly complete relief and rescue operations and ensure better treatment for the injured," he said in a post.

Boat accidents are a common occurrence in India where safety measures are deficient.

Skip next section Jantar Mantar: What to know about Delhi's delisted protest site?

Jantar Mantar: What to know about Delhi's delisted protest site?

Jantar Mantar, in central Delhi, is an 18th century open-air astronomical observatory.

For over three decades, a stretch of road leading up to it was where Indians came to be heard, press their demands and hold those in power accountable. That was until last week when the Delhi Police delisted the iconic venue as a protest site.

What sparked the latest protests?

The move came days after a confrontation between thousands of police personnel and anti-government protesters led by India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

The group, along with student organizations and activists, mobilized thousands to protest against a revision in electoral rolls which reportedly deleted 130 million voters.

While those deleted include dead and duplicate voters, critics argue the staggering number likely includes a vast number of eligible voters. India's poll body and the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party party have denied this.

Jantar Mantar has been the central rallying location for protesters demanding election Chief Gyanesh Kumar's resignation for overseeing the revision.

This is the same location that acted as a home base for the CJP-led youth protests in July over an exam scandal, which resulted in the removal of India's former education minister.

Why is delisting Jantar Mantar controversial?

Now, instead of Jantar Mantar, authorities have designated three alternative venues in Delhi. Campaigners argue those venues will reduce visibility and proximity to lawmakers as Jantar Mantar was surrounded by the nation's biggest institutions.

"Jantar Mantar is in the centre of the town, it is connected, it is next to parliament... it was a very important space for all protests," human rights activist Shabnam Hashmi told AFP. "This is nothing but a move to curb dissent," he said.

CJP leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das were among about a dozen people who jumped barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of Jantar Mantar, despite the delisting a day earlier.

An Indian court has now sent Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody over trespassing and other violations.

Skip next section Student organization demands 'immediate release' of Cockroach leaders

Student organization demands 'immediate release' of Cockroach leaders

Left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) on Wednesday demanded the "immediate release" of Cockroach movement conveners Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka after the duo were sent to judicial custody over trespassing amid protests.

"Tihar Jail for raising the Tricolor at Jantar Mantar?" the organization questioned in a post on X, adding that they stood in solidarity with the political pressure Group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP).

AISA is one among several groups and opposition parties protesting in India's national capital against India's election chief Gyanesh Kumar.

AISA's National President Neha Bora has been at the forefront of the recent protests which saw Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling government deploy thousands of police and rapid action forces to detain protesters. 

Skip next section Cockroach party conveners Ranka, Das sent to 5 days in judicial custody

Cockroach party conveners Ranka, Das sent to 5 days in judicial custody

Three leaders of India's Cockroach movement — Co-Conveners Saurav Das, Ashutosh Ranka and organizer Ajinkya Shinde — have been formally charged with multiple violations by authorities in India's national capital.

It all comes amid their protest against India's election chief over mass deletion of voter names from electoral rolls.

The trio was detained early Tuesday after they allegedly "sneaked" past police barricades to enter the grounds of Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which until recently was a designated protest site.

News agency PTI, citing sources, reported that police have now formally charged them with trespassing, violation of prohibitory orders, breach of a peace bond and obstructing a public servant from discharging officials duties.

Meanwhile, Cockroach Janta Party's Founder Abhijeet Dipke said Das and Ranka had been "sent to five days judicial custody."

"Their fault? Unfurling tricolor at Jantar Mantar," Dipke wrote on X on Wednesday morning, referring to the national flag.

"Show some guts, Narendra Modi. If you're so determined to crush dissent, have the courage to officially declare an Emergency instead of hiding behind these cowardly tactics," he said.

Dipke's post suggests the trio have already been produced in front of a magistrate. Under Indian law, a person arrested by police has to appear in court within 24 hours of the arrest. One can only be sent to judicial remand by a judge.

Defending advocate accuses police of making false claims in court

Advocate Abhisht Hela, who is representing Das and Ranka, questioned the grounds for sending the two into judicial remand and accused the police of making false claims in court, Times of India reported.

"They have been sent to five-day judicial custody because of the presumption of the police that they can commit a crime. Police lied in court that they had given a call urging people to come there," Hela said, adding that no such call was made.

Meanwhile, Shinde, who seems to have been released, told reporters that the government was misusing its powers to curtail people's rights. "If the government thinks that sending our two leaders, Ashutosh and Saurav, to jail for five days will frighten them, it is absolutely mistaken," Shinde said, as per PTI.

He further called on "everyone" to "come together to bring an end to this dictatorial government."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage!

Welcome to our coverage!

Good morning and welcome to DW's India blog.

This is Mahima Kapoor from Studio Delhi, ready to bring you the latest updates from India. The country has seen massive protests over reports of misconduct and pro-government bias by India's election chief. Mass detentions have followed in response to the demonstrations.

Leaders of India's Cockroach movement are facing formal charges after they "sneaked" into the Jantar Mantar grounds in central Delhi, which until recently was a designated protest site. Two of the Cockroach Janta Party conveners have been sent to five days in jail over charges of trespassing and obstructing official duties.

In other news, a boat on river Ganges capsized in India's eastern state of Bihar, killing at least 13 people. Most of the dead were children. Rescue operations are reportedly still ongoing.

On the international front, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to visit India next week to strengthen "strategic partnership" and discuss "enhanced energy cooperation." This will be Rubio's second official visit to India this year. 

Stay tuned as it's likely to be a news-heavy day.
